title: Jaidev, the old poet
hook: the poet of the Gita Govinda has two hymns in the Granth (Gujri, Jaidev, ang 526)

segments.voice: Yesterday, bemukh: O mind, leave the company of those turned away. Your line was one line. Which company did you give an hour to? Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

The Gita Govinda is a love poem in Sanskrit about Krishna and Radha: longing, quarrels, reunion in the forest by the river. Its poet is Jaidev. Now open the Guru Granth Sahib to Raag Gujri, Ang 526, and there is that same name at the head of a hymn. And it isn't the only one: Jaidev has two hymns in the Granth. The singer of the forest romance, sitting on the same pages as the Gurus.
screen: `A LOVE POEM: KRISHNA AND RADHA.` → `THE SAME NAME IN RAAG GUJRI.` → `TWO HYMNS IN THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: Start with how the Gujri hymn sounds. Its language leans hard on Sanskrit, the old learned tongue, so when it's sung it has a different ring from the Punjabi and Hindi around it. Same book, older accent. Now what it says. In paraphrase: the Lord was there before everything, beyond compare, true, lovely beyond telling, beyond nature itself. Then the turn. Chant only the Name of the Lord, which is sweet, the very essence of nectar. Remember Him, and the fear of birth, old age and death no longer has a hold. Then he gets practical. In paraphrase again, he asks for purity in three places at once: in what you do, what you say, and what you think. Not one of the three. All of them, lined up. Set that beside his fame. The poet known for a lush romance of gods in a forest is kept in the Granth for something spare: one Lord, beyond compare, and the Name. The hymn even asks, in paraphrase, what yoga, sacrifice, charity or austerity are worth beside that devotion. Just remembrance, and a life that matches it in deed, word and thought. Some readers hear the Gurus keeping the part of an old poet's voice that rings with their own. Others say simply that the Granth honors devotion wherever it was sung. Either way, an old name sits on the page, sung in the same kirtan as everything else, asking for one life lined up three ways: what you do, what you say, what you think.
screen: `AN OLDER ACCENT: SANSKRIT IN THE SOUND.` · `BEFORE EVERYTHING, BEYOND COMPARE.` · `THE NAME, AND NO FEAR OF DEATH.` · `PURE IN DEED, WORD AND THOUGHT.` · then, large: `THE OLD POET.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one of them. Not now, but after the sit, find Jaidev's Gujri hymn on Ang 526 in a translation you trust, and read it slowly, once. For the sit itself, take his three places. On one breath, think of something you did today. On the next, something you said. On the next, something you thought. Just look at each, gently, and keep the cycle going. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Jaidev. The poet of the Gita Govinda, whose hymns in the Granth praise the one Lord beyond compare and the sweet Name.
Your line: the old poet. Today, once, check that what you do, what you say and what you think are pointing the same way. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Jaidev's hymns are sung in kirtan in Raag Gujri and Raag Maru like other Gurbani, and Sikh readers hear in them the remembrance of the one Lord and the Name.

notes: Paraphrase of the Gujri hymn (parmaadi purakh manopimaṅ...; keval raam naam manoramaṅ; badi amrit tat maiaṅ; janam jaraadhi maran bhaiaṅ) and of the line on purity in deed, word and thought (man kram bachan): confirm.
'Its language leans hard on Sanskrit': confirm this is a fair description of the Gujri hymn.
Index hook says two hymns in the Granth (Gujri and Maru, Ang 1106 for the second): confirm Ang for Maru.
Identity of the Granth's Jaidev with the author of the Gita Govinda is from the index; tradition holds it, some scholars discuss it. Confirm phrasing.
'No temple, no image, no ritual in the hymn': confirm for the Gujri hymn.

Editor pass: cut 'from far outside Punjab' (a place claim not in the cited text), replaced the closing slogan with a concrete restatement of deed, word and thought, and varied the hook ending, a 'Here's' teach turn and the practice opener.

Audit (2026-10-01): removed 'No temple, no image, no ritual in the hymn', which is wrong as stated: the Gujri hymn names yoga, sacrifice, charity and austerity (jogen kin jagen kin daanen kin tapasaa) to set them below devotion. Replaced with a paraphrase of that line. The deed, word and thought line is rid karmanaa bachasaa (heart, deed, word): confirm 'purity' for nihkevala.
